In reality, as the body of the story makes clear, it really is just like the rest of prohibition, a counterproductive fraud that has taken on a life of its own.

It has a massive, politically powerful constituency, in this case thousands of local police forces around the country. They love D.A.R.E. And why not? It is a very pleasant job. It certainly beats going out and chasing dangerous criminals. In stead, it takes them into the schools where they can indoctrinate children to trust the police more than their parents and even to report their parents to the police.

The story says that the reason that D.A.R.E. is counterproductive is a "mystery." It is only a "mystery" to those committed to the prohibitionist paradigm.

Consider the way the report begins: "

Does a "drug-free life" exclude alcohol when they are adults? Ritalin or Prozac when they are prescribed by doctors? Is the pledge binding when they find out that they have been lied to? These are not frivolous ethical questions.

Consider the other pledge that they take: "The Pledge of Allegiance." Aren’t all pledges demeaned by this deceit? Remember that the D.A.R.E. pledge is administered by officials who represent the state ideology of the US. The Pledge of Allegiance may be taught by mere teachers or private citizens.

Substantively, can anyone be surprised that children react negatively when they find out that they have been lied to. I repeatedly quote what I have been told again and again over more than two decades: "When I found out that they had lied to me about marijuana, I thought that they had lied to me about everything else."

If people cannot bring themselves to admit that we have been lying to kids about marijuana, then the reason why D.A.R.E. and other such programs are counterproductive will remain a "mystery," not a clue for the clueless.)

Is D.A.R.E. losing drug war?  Critics say program fails to stop drug abuse

NBC NEWS "I pledge to lead a drug-free life." For more than 23 million children, and 80 percent of America’s schools, this is the nation’s anti-drug mantra. It’s part of a program called D.A.R.E. But as NBC’s Jim Avila reports, some critics are questioning whether D.A.R.E. is worth the millions of dollars spent on it each year.      Reporter Jim Avila

IT’S CALLED D.A.R.E. — Drug Abuse Resistance Education — and it’s one of the most popular subjects in Mrs. Blackwell’s fifth-grade class in the Chapel Hill, N.C., school district. A local police officer leads the class in reciting the D.A.R.E. pledge. But even though it’s popular, Chapel Hill is thinking about dropping the D.A.R.E. class, for one simple reason — compelling evidence that it does not work, does not stop drug abuse.

"The body of research about D.A.R.E. says that it has no long-term effect for drug abuse prevention," says school system health director Susan Spalt.

There has been lots of research about D.A.R.E., conducted by lots of experts. For its part, D.A.R.E. embraces one study from Ohio State that says that D.A.R.E. does work if students are given additional anti-drug classes through high school. But an overwhelming majority of students are not. ‘Kids in the suburbs ... who participated in D.A.R.E. actually had significantly higher levels of drug use than suburban kids who did not get the D.A.R.E. program.’

DR. DENNIS ROSENBAUM University of Illinois And a dozen other studies flatly conclude: D.A.R.E. does not deliver on its promise to "teach kids to resist drugs."

And now another study, the most comprehensive yet. It follows 1,800 Illinois kids from fifth grade through high school — using research techniques endorsed by D.A.R.E. itself. Its author says there’s no doubt about it: D.A.R.E. is a waste of money — $220 million in tax money and donations last year alone, with no beneficial effect on student drug use.

"It hurts me to sit here and tell you that D.A.R.E. does not work," says Dr. Dennis Rosenbaum, head of the criminal justice department at the University of Illinois. "But it’s time for us to go back to the drawing board and figure out how it can be improved or what better ways we can spend our money on drug education in this country."

Rosenbaum’s six-year study found that kids in the core D.A.R.E. program use the same amount of drugs as those not in D.A.R.E. But perhaps the researchers most surprising conclusion: D.A.R.E. actually appears to have an "adverse" effect on drug activity in suburban communities.

"Kids in the suburbs who were exposed to the D.A.R.E. program, who participated in D.A.R.E., actually had significantly higher levels of drug use than suburban kids who did not get the D.A.R.E. program," Rosenbaum said. "This was very disturbing to us."

It’s a mystery the researchers say needs further study.

"Kids in the suburbs who were exposed to the D.A.R.E. program, who participated in D.A.R.E., actually had significantly higher levels of drug use than suburban kids who did not get the D.A.R.E. program," Rosenbaum said. "This was very disturbing to us."

It’s a mystery the researchers say needs further study.

NBC News provided a copy of the study to D.A.R.E. spokesman Bill Alden, a former U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency agent, and asked him about the adverse effect.

"I have no idea," Alden said. "I don’t know — I don’t have an answer."

In fact, D.A.R.E. believes schools need more D.A.R.E. And the group pushes to add additional programs in junior and high schools. "Its not that D.A.R.E. doesn’t work," Alden maintains. "D.A.R.E. does work. But it dissipates, it erodes. What has to happen — there has to be more, not less."

But the two key federal agencies evaluating drug abuse programs do not recommend D.A.R.E. on their lists of acceptable programs, leaving school districts like Chapel Hill with a difficult choice. D.A.R.E. is a popular program.

"We’ve got thousands and thousands of principals, millions of parents saying, ‘D.A.R.E. made a difference in my child’s life — I like D.A.R.E.,’ " argues D.A.R.E.’s Alden. (Ed. note: This is what would be called "anecdotal evidence in another context.)

The choice — continue to bring D.A.R.E.’s friendly police officers into the classroom or replace D.A.R.E. because of mounting evidence the program does not work.
